::: {#exm-racket-bfs}
#### Breadth-first search in Racket

This Racket version of `bfs` (@def-bfs) keeps the labels in a list of pairs `(list u d)`,
one for each marked vertex $u$ with label $d$,
so a vertex is marked when `assoc` (@exr-racket-assoc) finds it in that list.
It uses `neighbors` from @exm-racket-neighbors.

```{racket}
#| code-fold: false
(define (unmarked vs dist)
  (if (empty? vs)
      empty
      (if (assoc (first vs) dist)
          (unmarked (rest vs) dist)
          (cons (first vs) (unmarked (rest vs) dist)))))

(define (label vs d)
  (if (empty? vs)
      empty
      (cons (list (first vs) d) (label (rest vs) d))))

(define (bfs-loop G queue dist)
  (if (empty? queue)
      dist
      (let* ([v (first queue)]
             [new (unmarked (neighbors G v) dist)]
             [d (+ 1 (second (assoc v dist)))])
        (bfs-loop G
                  (append (rest queue) new)
                  (append dist (label new d))))))

(define (bfs G s)
  (bfs-loop G (list s) (list (list s 0))))
```

- `(unmarked vs dist)` keeps the vertices of the list `vs` that have no label yet.
- `(label vs d)` pairs each vertex of `vs` with the label `d`.
- `(let* ([x e] ...) body)` evaluates `e`, calls its value `x` inside the rest of the `let*`, and then evaluates `body`.
- `(append L M)` is the list of the elements of `L` followed by those of `M`,
  so `(append (rest queue) new)` removes the front of the queue and adds the new vertices at the back.

Each call of `bfs-loop` is one pass through the loop of @def-bfs.
From $a$, it returns the marks and labels of @exm-bfs-trace:

```{racket}
#| code-fold: false
(bfs office 'a)
```

:::
